title: The motor effect — force on a current-carrying wire
examTip: Fleming's left-hand rule is for the motor effect: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Thumb = thrust (force), index finger = field, middle finger = current. All three must be at right angles to each other.
introTips: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force. This is the motor effect.
Fleming's left-hand rule tells you the direction of the force. Thumb = force, index = field, middle = current.
The force is greatest when the current and magnetic field are perpendicular. It is zero when they are parallel.
More current, a stronger field or a longer conductor all increase the force.
The electric motor uses the motor effect. The split-ring commutator keeps it spinning without stopping.
intro: Every electric motor in the world works because of a discovery from the early 1800s. That includes the tiny one in your phone's vibration alert and the huge ones driving electric trains. A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a force. This is the motor effect. It is the bridge between electricity and motion. Once you understand it, you will see it everywhere: in electric vehicles, loudspeakers and factory machines. The force on a single wire is small. But put hundreds of turns of wire in a strong magnetic field. Then you get a lot of torque. It is enough to accelerate a car from 0 to 60 mph in under three seconds.

keyPoints.heading: The motor effect — force on a current-carrying conductor
keyPoints.content: When an electric current flows through a conductor inside a magnetic field, the conductor feels a force. This is called the motor effect. The force acts perpendicular to both the current direction and the magnetic field direction. The force is zero if the current flows parallel to the magnetic field. To feel a force, the conductor must run at least partly across the field. The direction of the force reverses if: (a) the direction of the current is reversed, or (b) the direction of the magnetic field is reversed. Reversing both at once keeps the force in the same direction. This effect is how electric motors, loudspeakers and galvanometers work.
writeBullets: Motor effect — a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force
Force is perpendicular to both the current direction and the magnetic field
No force if the current is parallel to the field. It must run at least partly across the field
Reversing the current OR the field reverses the force. Reversing both leaves the force unchanged
The basis of electric motors, loudspeakers and galvanometers

keyTerms.def: The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field; force is perpendicular to both current and field
A region of space where a magnetic force acts on moving charged particles or current-carrying conductors

keyPoints.memTip: Motor effect = current + magnetic field → force. The three quantities (force, current, field) are always at right angles to each other.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often think the force acts along the current or the field. It is always perpendicular to both. That is why a wire moves sideways out of a magnetic field.

keyPoints.heading: Fleming's left-hand rule
keyPoints.content: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force (motion) on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Use your left hand: - point your index finger in the direction of the magnetic Field (from the N to the S pole) - point your middle finger in the direction of conventional Current (from + to −, the way positive charges would flow) - your thumb then points in the direction of the Thrust (the force on the conductor) All three fingers must be held at right angles to each other. Memory aid: FBI. Force (thumb), B-field (index) and Current (middle; think 'I' for current). Always use conventional current (from + to −), not electron flow.
writeBullets: Fleming's left-hand rule — the left hand is for the motor effect
Index finger → magnetic Field direction (N to S)
Middle finger → Current direction (conventional, + to −)
Thumb → Thrust (the direction of force or motion)
All three fingers must be at 90° to each other

keyTerms.def: A mnemonic using the left hand to determine the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor: thumb=force, index=field, middle=current
Current defined as flowing from positive to negative terminal — the direction positive charges would flow; opposite to electron flow

keyPoints.memTip: FBI left hand: Force (thumb), B-field (index finger), I-current (middle finger). Left hand = motor effect.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Really hold up your left hand and point your fingers. Picturing the directions is harder than the rule itself. Most mistakes come from using the wrong hand or not holding the fingers at 90°.

keyPoints.heading: Factors affecting the size of the force: F = BIL
keyPoints.content: The size of the force on a current-carrying conductor is given by: F = BIL. - F = force (N) - B = magnetic flux density (tesla, T). This is how strong the magnetic field is. - I = current (A) - L = length of conductor in the field (m) The force increases if you: - increase the current (I) - use a stronger magnet (higher B) - use a longer conductor in the field (L) Worked example: a wire of length 0.5 m carries a current of 3 A in a field of B = 0.2 T. Force = 0.2 × 3 × 0.5 = 0.3 N. Rearrangements: B = F ÷ (IL), I = F ÷ (BL), L = F ÷ (BI).
writeBullets: F = BIL: Force (N) = magnetic flux density (T) × current (A) × length (m)
Larger B (stronger magnet) → larger force
Larger I (more current) → larger force
Larger L (a longer conductor in the field) → larger force
Rearrangements: B = F/(IL); I = F/(BL); L = F/(BI)

keyTerms.def: The equation for force on a current-carrying conductor: F = magnetic flux density × current × length in the field
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field; unit: tesla (T)

keyPoints.memTip: F = BIL: 'Bill the force'. Force equals B times I times L.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to rearrange F = BIL for all three variables. It is a required calculation, and rearranging is often tested.

keyPoints.heading: The electric motor and the loudspeaker
keyPoints.content: An electric motor uses the motor effect to turn electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy. A coil of wire (the armature) sits in a magnetic field. When current flows, the two sides of the coil feel forces in opposite directions. This follows from Fleming's left-hand rule on each side. So the coil rotates. The problem: if the current direction stays the same, the forces reverse after half a turn, and the motor stops. The split-ring commutator solves this. It reverses the current direction in the coil every half turn. So the forces always push the same way round, and the motor keeps spinning. To increase motor speed or torque, increase the current or the field strength. Or add more turns of wire, or use an iron core. A loudspeaker also uses the motor effect. Alternating current flows through a coil in a magnetic field. This makes the coil move back and forth. The coil pushes a cone, which makes sound waves.
writeBullets: Electric motor — a coil in a magnetic field. Its opposite sides feel opposite forces → rotation
Split-ring commutator — reverses the current every half turn. Keeps the motor spinning
To increase speed or torque: more current, a stronger field, more coil turns, an iron core
Loudspeaker — AC through a coil in a magnetic field → the coil oscillates → the cone vibrates → sound
A motor turns electrical energy → rotational kinetic energy

keyTerms.def: A device that uses the motor effect to convert electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy
A device in a DC electric motor that reverses the current in the coil every half turn, maintaining continuous rotation
The rotating coil in an electric motor

keyPoints.memTip: The commutator 'commutes' (reverses) the current every half turn. So the motor keeps going the same way. Without it, the motor would rock back and forth.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often describe the commutator as 'making more electricity'. In fact, it reverses the direction of the current that is already there. That keeps the rotation going round, instead of rocking.

0.question: A current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field. In Fleming's left-hand rule, which finger shows the direction of the magnetic field?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! Index finger = Field (B). Thumb = Force (thrust). Middle finger = Current (I). Remember: FBI.
0.wrongFeedback: In Fleming's left-hand rule: index finger = Field, middle finger = Current, thumb = Force (thrust). FBI: Force, B-field, I-current.

1.question: A wire of length 0.4 m carries a current of 5 A. It is in a magnetic field of flux density 0.3 T. What is the force on the wire?
1.wrongFeedback: Use F = BIL: force = 0.3 (T) × 5 (A) × 0.4 (m) = 0.6 N. Write the formula first, then substitute, then calculate.

3.question: Why does an electric motor have a split-ring commutator?
options: To reverse the current direction every half turn, so the motor keeps spinning
To increase the voltage supplied to the motor
To stop the coil from overheating
To turn alternating current into direct current
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Without the commutator, the forces would reverse after half a turn. The coil would rock back and forth. The commutator reverses the current to keep it rotating.
3.wrongFeedback: The split-ring commutator reverses the current direction in the coil every half turn. This keeps the motor force pushing the same way round. So the coil keeps spinning.

commonMistakes: Using the right hand instead of the left for the motor effect. Fleming's left-hand rule is for the motor effect. The right hand is for the generator effect (induction).
Using the direction of electron flow instead of conventional current in Fleming's rule. Conventional current flows from + to −. Always use it when applying the rule.
Saying the force acts along the current or the field. The force is always perpendicular to both. It acts in the third perpendicular direction.
Forgetting units in F = BIL calculations. Force is in newtons, flux density in tesla, current in amps and length in metres.
Saying the commutator 'increases speed'. The commutator keeps the rotation going. It does not increase the speed. That needs more current or a stronger field.
examTips: Always hold up your real left hand when using Fleming's left-hand rule. It is very easy to mix up directions if you don't.
For F = BIL questions, write the formula first. Then substitute values with units, then calculate. Method marks are available.
In motor questions, always explain what the split-ring commutator does. It reverses the current every half turn to keep the rotation going.
If the current or the field reverses, say clearly how this changes the direction of the force.
For loudspeaker questions, explain the chain: AC current → alternating force → oscillating coil → vibrating cone → sound wave.
